note: A mock-heroic opening. Dante lists, in the grand manner, every military signal he has ever heard, only to say that none was as strange as the one that ended the last canto: the devil captain's fart.

In the Italian Dante speaks to the people of Arezzo directly: he has seen riders in their land. In June 1289 Florence and its Guelph allies defeated Arezzo at Campaldino, and Dante is believed to have fought there in the cavalry.
Italian cities took a bell to war, mounted on the carroccio, the ox-drawn wagon that carried the city's standard.
The Italian names a reed pipe. It is the signal Barbariccia gave at the end of Canto 21.
The patrol that Malacoda picked in Canto 21 to see the poets to the next bridge. Barbariccia leads it.

quote: saints in the church and gluttons in the tavern
note: A proverb: you keep the company the place gives you. In Hell that means devils.
The boiling tar that fills the fifth ditch of Malebolge. Under it are the grafters, who took bribes in public office.
Sailors believed that dolphins leaping near a ship were a sign that a storm was coming.
The sinners here are compared to one small animal after another: dolphins, frogs, an otter, a mouse, a duck. The canto is told as a comic chase, the lightest in the Inferno.
"Curly-beard", the leader of the ten devils. Later lines call him their captain and the grand provost. He keeps his squad in check, more or less.
"Dog-scratcher", one of the ten.
Otters were hunted with spears and hooks and pulled from the water, sleek and black.

quote: I already knew all their names
note: Malacoda called the ten by name in Canto 21. Dante explains how he can tell them apart, as a careful witness would.
"Red-face", described as raging when he was picked for the patrol.

A small kingdom on both sides of the western Pyrenees, between France and Spain. The speaker never gives his name. Early commentators call him Ciampolo, an Italian form of Jean-Paul, and nothing is known of him beyond what he says here.
Thibaut II, king of Navarre from 1253 to 1270 and also count of Champagne, remembered as a just ruler. He died on the way home from the crusade against Tunis.
The Italian word is baratteria, barratry: selling the favors of a public post. As a trusted servant of the king, he sold what was in the king's gift.
"Hog". His boar's tusks were mentioned when he was chosen.

quote: Stand back while I skewer him properly
note: In the Italian Barbariccia is not about to stab him. He holds the sinner pinned in his arms and tells the others to keep off while he does, so that Virgil can go on with his questions.
The Italian word is "latino", Latin, Dante's usual word for an Italian. Virgil asks because Dante will want news of his own countrymen.
Sardinia, near Italy. In Dante's time most of the island was controlled by Pisa and Genoa.
Another of the ten devils. His name may combine two winds, the libeccio and the sirocco.
A name that suggests a big, ugly dragon.

A Sardinian friar who served as deputy to Nino Visconti of Pisa, the ruler of Gallura. He took bribes to let his master's prisoners escape, and Nino had him hanged. Nino himself, a friend of Dante's, appears among the saved in Purgatorio 8.
The northeastern part of Sardinia. The island was divided into four districts called judicatures, each under a ruler with the title of judge.

context: The Navarrese gives no details of his crimes, only that he and Friar Gomita talk endlessly of home.

note: Logudoro, the northwestern judicature of Sardinia.
Barbariccia again, given a mock title of rank.
His name was a word for a goblin or imp in Italian folklore.
People from central and northern Italy. He offers what he guesses these two travelers would most like to see, since he has heard them speak.

context: The sinner asks them to step back out of sight. It is the opening move of his trick.

note: He offers to betray seven of his fellow sinners to save himself. Whether he would really have done it is left open. A grafter makes a deal even with devils.
The all-clear signal, he says, that the sinners use when one of them comes up and finds no devils near.
"Nasty dog". He is the one devil who sees the trick for what it is.

quote: Too cunning by far, I am
note: Mock innocence. He pretends that the only wickedness in his plan is toward his friends below, whom he would be handing over to the hooks.
The devil whose name may be related to Harlequin. He can't resist a sporting bet: a race between his wings and the sinner's legs.

quote: use the bank as a screen
note: He is speaking to the other devils now. They are to leave the top of the bank and go down behind it, so that they are hidden from the pitch and the sinner gets a fair start.

quote: Reader, you're about to hear a new game!
note: Dante speaks to the reader like a storyteller in the square announcing the best part. The deceivers are about to be deceived, and by one of their own prisoners.

quote: the one most reluctant to play
note: Cagnazzo, who had smelled the trick. Even he turns away.
The only name the poem gives him.

quote: the one who'd caused the blunder
note: Alichino, who proposed the bet.
Hunting with falcons was the sport of medieval nobles, and Dante takes many comparisons from it. A falcon that misses its strike flies back up sullen and tired.
"Frost-trampler", another of the ten. He wants the sinner to get away, so that he will have an excuse to attack Alichino.
The devils end up in their own pitch, like the sinners they guard. Fraud turns on itself: the grafter cheats the devils, and the devils fall to fighting each other.
The poets slip away while the patrol is busy. The devils will blame them for the mishap and come after them at the start of the next canto.
